title: Why Sleep Might Not be as Restorative as We Get Older - Nautilus
gist: An MIT-led Nature Aging study using fMRI, CSF-flow MRI and EEG found older adults (60–84) have markedly weaker sleep-driven cerebrospinal fluid pulses than young adults, suggesting reduced nightly brain waste clearance with age.

insights.claim: During sleep, slow brain waves trigger pulses of cerebrospinal fluid that flush out waste accumulated during the day, a process linked to cognitive health, neuroprotection and memory consolidation.
insights.so_what: Underpins interest in sleep-targeted interventions for neurodegeneration.
insights.locator: As you’re sleeping, slow brain waves
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: An MIT-led study in Nature Aging scanning young (18–39) and older (60–84) volunteers overnight with fMRI, CSF-flow MRI and EEG found that CSF pulses tracked intensifying slow waves in the young but were markedly weaker in older participants.
insights.so_what: Points to age-related clearance decline as a target for sleep-tech and neuro-therapeutics.
insights.quote: Among the older participants, however, these CSF waves were markedly weaker.
insights.locator: A team of neuroscientists led by
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
